subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will meet solid shapes. You will name the cube, the sphere and the cylinder, find their faces, edges and curved surfaces, and discover which shapes roll and which stack. Then you will meet flat shapes — the circle, square, triangle and rectangle — and count their sides and corners.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Name common 3D shapes: cube, sphere and cylinder.
Talk about the faces, edges and curved surfaces of a 3D shape.
Say which 3D shapes can roll and which can stack.
Name common 2D shapes: circle, square, rectangle and triangle.
Count the sides of a 2D shape and find its corners.
Tell the difference between straight and curved sides.
Sort shapes into groups by a property (rolls / stacks, straight / curved).
Spot and name shapes in everyday objects at home and outside.
A ball or an orange (a sphere).
Fold a shape in half to check whether both sides match exactly, and know this is called symmetry. Make and continue a simple repeating pattern using 2D shapes, such as circle, square, circle, square.

concepts.title: Meeting 3D Shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder)
concepts.explanation: Start with real solid objects, not pictures. A 3D shape is one you can hold in their hand – it takes up space and has depth. Gather three things: a ball (sphere), a tin or tube (cylinder), and a box or die (cube). Pick each one up, turn it over, and feel it before you name it.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Hand the child the ball and say its name: ‘This is a sphere. It is round all over.’ Do the same with the cube (‘a box shape with flat sides’) and the cylinder (‘like a tin – flat circles at the ends and a curved side’). Then muddle the three objects and ask the child to pass you ‘the sphere’, ‘the cube’, ‘the cylinder’. Turn each shape to a new position and name it again, so you learn that turning a shape does not change its name.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Hold the ball. Is it round all over, or does it have flat sides?” Child: “Round all over!” You: “Yes — a shape that is round all over is a sphere.” You: “Now hold the tin. Find the flat round part. Find the curved part. This shape is a cylinder.”

concepts.title: Faces, Edges and Curved Surfaces
concepts.explanation: Once you can name the three shapes, describe the parts. A face is a flat part you can lay on the table. An edge is the line where two faces meet. A curved surface is a smooth, rounded part with no corners at all.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Give the child a cube and count the flat faces together as you turn it – there are 6, and each one is a square. Run a finger along an edge and say the word. Then give the child the sphere: it has no flat faces and no edges, just one curved surface – that is why it rolls so easily. The cylinder is a nice in-between: it has 2 flat round faces (top and bottom) and 1 curved surface around the middle.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us count the flat faces on the cube. Touch each one as we count.” Child and you: “One, two, three, four, five, six.” You: “Six flat faces, and every one is a square. Now feel the ball — can you find a flat face? No! It is curved all over.”

concepts.title: Rolling and Stacking
concepts.explanation: This is a favourite, because you can test it. The rule is simple: a shape can roll if it has a curved surface, and a shape can stack if it has flat faces to sit on.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Gently tip each shape on the floor or a tray. The sphere rolls everywhere (curved all over). The cube stacks and does not roll (all flat faces). The cylinder does both – it rolls on its curved side and stacks when stood on a flat end. Then build a little tower together and talk about which shape is best at the bottom (a cube – it will not roll away) and which is tricky at the top.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Give the ball a little push. What does it do?” Child: “It rolls!” You: “Why does it roll?” Child: “Because it is round.” You: “Now try the box. Does it roll?” Child: “No, it stays still.” You: “Right — flat faces let it stack instead of roll.”

concepts.title: Meeting 2D Shapes (circle, square, rectangle, triangle)
concepts.explanation: A 2D shape is flat – you can draw it on paper, but you cannot pick it up off the page. A good way to meet 2D shapes is to draw around the flat faces of the solid objects: draw around the end of the tin to make a circle, or around one face of the box to make a square.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Introduce the four shapes one at a time, always with a real example. The circle is round like a plate and has 1 curved side with no corners. The square has 4 straight sides all the same length and 4 corners. The rectangle also has 4 straight sides and 4 corners, but it is longer one way – its opposite sides are the same length, like a door. The triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners, like the pointed top of a roof.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “This plate is a circle. Trace the edge with your finger — round and round, no corners.” You: “Now the window. Count the sides: one, two, three, four. All the same length — that makes it a square.” You: “Look at the roof top. How many sides?” Child: “Three!” You: “Three sides, three corners — a triangle.”

concepts.title: Counting Sides and Corners; Straight or Curved
concepts.explanation: Now sharpen your eye for the properties that tell shapes apart. Counting sides is the key skill. Touch and count each side, and to mark a starting point so they do not go around twice.
concepts.example: Two ideas are worth repeating gently. First, turning a shape does not change it: a square tilted to look like a diamond is still a square. Second, triangles come in many shapes – tall thin ones, wide flat ones – and they are all triangles as long as they have exactly 3 straight sides.
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Lay out the four shapes. Together, touch and count the sides: circle 1 (a single curved side), triangle 3, square 4, rectangle 4. Then sort by side type: the circle has a curved side; the square, rectangle and triangle all have straight sides only. Find the corners too – the circle has none, the triangle has 3, and the square and rectangle each have 4.

concepts.title: Sorting Shapes and Finding Them in Everyday Objects
concepts.explanation: Sorting pulls the whole unit together. To sort is to put shapes into groups that share something the same – for example, ‘shapes that roll’ and ‘shapes that stack’, or ‘shapes with straight sides’ and ‘shapes with a curved side’.
concepts.example: Confusing square and rectangle. A square is a special rectangle where all four sides are equal. Compare a cracker (square) with a door (rectangle).
concepts.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Make two spaces on the floor or table (two mats, two hoops, or just two piles). Give the child a handful of objects and shape cards and ask them to sort by one rule at a time. Say the rule out loud: ‘This pile is for shapes that can roll. This pile is for shapes that can stack.’ Then go on a shape hunt around the home – a round plate, a rectangle door, a tin cylinder, the square of a floor tile. Naming shapes in real life is the strongest sign you truly understands them. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Let us hunt for circles. Can you find something round and flat like a plate?” Child: “The clock! And the bottom of the cup!” You: “Wonderful hunting. Now let us find a rectangle — something with four straight sides, longer one way.” Mixing up 2D and 3D names – calling a cube a ‘square’ or a sphere a ‘circle’. Remember: you can hold a 3D shape; a 2D shape is flat on the paper. Trace a face of the box to show the square hiding inside the cube. Thinking a turned shape changes its name. A square tipped onto a corner looks like a diamond but is still a square. Turn shapes often and re-name them. Believing all triangles look the same. Show tall, wide and lopsided triangles – all are triangles if they have 3 straight sides.

concepts.title: Line Symmetry and Simple Shape Patterns
concepts.explanation: A shape has line symmetry when you can fold it exactly in half and both sides match perfectly, like looking in a mirror. Some shapes have symmetry and some do not.
concepts.grownUpGuide:
How to teach it: Cut a paper circle, square, rectangle and triangle. Fold each one in half. Ask yourself, 'Do the two sides land exactly on top of each other?' A circle folded through its middle always matches. A square folded corner to corner or side to side also matches. Some shapes, like a triangle cut with uneven sides, might not match when folded — talk about why. Butterflies, leaves and many faces are symmetrical too; look for real examples around the house. Once you have explored symmetry, move to shape patterns: lay out a simple repeating row such as circle, square, circle, square, circle, ___ and ask what comes next. Patterns can also use size or colour, but keep the shapes themselves the star of the show here.

🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Fold this paper circle exactly in half. Do the two sides match?” Child: “Yes!” You: “That means the circle has symmetry — folding it makes two matching halves.” You: “Now look at this pattern: circle, square, circle, square, circle... What comes next?” Child: “Square!” You: “Well done — you spotted the pattern.”

explorations.title: Meeting 3D Shapes (cube, sphere, cylinder)
explorations.context: Start with real solid objects, not pictures. A 3D shape is one you can hold in their hand – it takes up space and has depth. Gather three things: a ball (sphere), a tin or tube (cylinder), and a box or die (cube).
explorations.prompt: Hold a ball and a box in your hands. Which one is round all over with no flat parts?
explorations.hint: Feel each one - does it have any flat sides you could lay on a table?
explorations.explanation: Notice that each shape's name is tied to how it feels in the hand, not just how it looks in a picture — round all over for the sphere, flat sides for the cube, and flat ends with a curved side in between for the cylinder. Handle and name all three several times before testing them mixed up and out of order.

explorations.title: Faces, Edges and Curved Surfaces
explorations.context: Once you can name the three shapes, describe the parts. A face is a flat part you can lay on the table. An edge is the line where two faces meet. A curved surface is a smooth, rounded part with no corners at all.
explorations.prompt: Look at a cube, like a box or a die. How many flat faces does it have?
explorations.hint: Turn the cube in your hand and touch each flat side as you count.
explorations.explanation: Explain that a face is any flat part you could lay on a table, an edge is the line where two faces meet, and a curved surface has neither — which is exactly why the sphere, with only a curved surface, rolls in every direction while the cube, with six flat faces, does not roll at all.

explorations.title: Rolling and Stacking
explorations.context: This is a favourite, because you can test it. The rule is simple: a shape can roll if it has a curved surface, and a shape can stack if it has flat faces to sit on.
explorations.prompt: Give a ball and a box a gentle push on the floor. Which one rolls away?
explorations.hint: Think about which shape has a curved surface all over, and which has flat faces.
explorations.explanation: The rolling-and-stacking rule connects straight back to faces and curved surfaces: anything with a curved surface can roll, and anything with flat faces can stack. A cube makes the steadiest base for a tower because all six of its faces are flat, while a sphere would simply roll away.
explorations.grownUpGuide: How to teach it: Gently tip each shape on the floor or a tray.

explorations.title: Meeting 2D Shapes (circle, square, rectangle, triangle)
explorations.context: A 2D shape is flat – you can draw it on paper, but you cannot pick it up off the page.
explorations.prompt: Look at a round plate and a folded paper triangle. Which shape has no straight sides at all?
explorations.hint: Trace around the edge of each shape with your finger - does it have any corners?
explorations.explanation: Point out that tracing around a flat face of a real object — the end of a tin for a circle, a face of a box for a square — connects the new 2D shape directly to the 3D object it came from. A square's four sides are all the same length, while a rectangle's four sides come in two matching pairs, one pair longer than the other.

explorations.title: Counting Sides and Corners; Straight or Curved
explorations.context: Now sharpen your eye for the properties that tell shapes apart. Counting sides is the key skill. Touch and count each side, and to mark a starting point so they do not go around twice.
explorations.prompt: Count the straight sides of a square and a triangle. How many sides does each one have?
explorations.hint: Touch each side once as you count around the shape, starting from the same corner.
explorations.explanation: Counting sides works best when you mark a starting point and touches each side exactly once going around, the same discipline used for counting objects. Sorting the shapes afterwards by straight or curved sides shows the circle stands apart — it is the only one here with no corners at all.

explorations.title: Sorting Shapes and Finding Them in Everyday Objects
explorations.context: Sorting pulls the whole unit together. To sort is to put shapes into groups that share something the same – for example, ‘shapes that roll’ and ‘shapes that stack’, or ‘shapes with straight sides’ and ‘shapes with a curved side’.
explorations.prompt: ⚽ → __________ 🟦 → __________ 🥫 → __________ Sort each picture by naming its shape.
explorations.hint: Think about which shapes roll and which have flat sides before naming each one.
explorations.explanation: Saying the sorting rule out loud before starting — ‘this pile is for shapes that roll, this pile is for shapes that stack’ — gives you a test to apply to each object rather than a guess. Finding a matching shape in a real object at home, like a round plate or a rectangular door, is the clearest sign the idea has truly stuck.

methods.title: Naming 3D Shapes by Touch
methods.example: Naming a ball, a tin, and a box
steps: Gather a ball, a tin can, and a box. Hold each one before naming it.
Say the name as you touch it: 'This ball is a sphere,' 'This tin is a cylinder,' 'This box is a cube.'
Mix the three objects up and name each one without help, checking each answer together.

methods.title: Counting Faces and Edges on a Cube
methods.example: Counting the six faces of a cube
steps: Take a cube — a box or a die — and find a flat part you can lay on the table. That is a face.
Turn the cube together and count all six faces out loud, touching each one.
Run a finger along the line where two faces meet and name it an edge; then compare with the sphere, which has no faces or edges at all.

methods.title: Testing Which Shapes Roll and Which Stack
methods.example: Rolling a ball, tin, and box on the floor
steps: Lay a ball, a tin, and a box on the floor and gently push each one in turn.
Watch what happens: the ball rolls away, the box stays still, and the tin rolls on its side but stands still on its flat end.
Sort the three objects into a 'rolls' pile and a 'stacks' pile, explaining why each belongs there.

methods.title: Naming 2D Shapes by Their Sides
methods.example: Naming a plate, a window, and a roof
steps: Look at a plate (circle), a window (square or rectangle), and a folded paper triangle.
Trace around each shape's edge with a finger, naming it as you go: 'round with no corners' for the circle, 'four equal sides' for the square.
Point to the one shape with no straight sides at all.

methods.title: Counting Sides and Corners on Flat Shapes
methods.example: Counting the four sides of a square tile
steps: Lay out a circle, a triangle, a square, and a rectangle cut from paper or card.
Touch and count each side out loud together, starting from the same corner so none are counted twice.
Record the count for each shape and ask yourself which shape had the fewest sides and which had a curved side instead of corners.

methods.title: Sorting Shapes by Straight or Curved Sides
methods.example: Sorting an orange, a book, and a can into two piles
steps: Collect a small pile of household objects and shape cards, mixed together.
Make two spaces on the table — one for 'straight sides' and one for 'curved sides' — and say the rule out loud.
Sort each object into a pile, then explain their reason for at least two of their choices.

workedExamples.title: Naming 3D shapes around the house
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a ball, a tin of beans, and a box of dates. Name the 3D shape of each object.
workedExamples.solution: The ball is round all over with no flat parts — it is a sphere. The tin has flat circles at each end and a curved side — it is a cylinder. The box of dates has six flat square faces — it is a cube.

workedExamples.title: Counting the flat faces of a cube
workedExamples.prompt: How many flat faces does a cube-shaped box of dates have, and what is the flat part called?
workedExamples.solution: Turn the box and touch each flat part — count them one at a time: one, two, three, four, five, six. Each flat part is called a face, so a cube has 6 faces in total.

workedExamples.title: Testing which shape rolls
workedExamples.prompt: Give a ball and a box of dates a gentle push on the floor. Which one rolls, and which one stacks?
workedExamples.solution: The ball is curved all over, so it rolls away easily. The box of dates has flat faces, so it does not roll — it stays still and can be stacked. The ball can roll; the box can stack.

workedExamples.title: Naming 2D shapes at home
workedExamples.prompt: Look at a round plate, a square floor tile, and a folded triangle of paper. Name each 2D shape.
workedExamples.solution: The plate is round with one curved side and no corners — it is a circle. The floor tile has four straight sides all the same length — it is a square. The folded paper has three straight sides — it is a triangle.

workedExamples.title: Counting the sides of a triangle and a rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: Count the sides of a triangle drawn on paper and the sides of a rectangle door. How many sides does each shape have?
workedExamples.solution: Touch and count the triangle's sides: one, two, three — a triangle has 3 straight sides. Now count the door's sides: one, two, three, four — a rectangle has 4 straight sides, with opposite sides the same length.

workedExamples.title: Matching everyday objects to shape names
workedExamples.solution: The ball ⚽ is round all over, so it is a sphere. The blue square 🟦 has 4 straight equal sides, so it is a square. The can 🥫 has flat round ends and a curved side, so it is a cylinder.

workedExamples.title: Which shape rolls and which stacks
workedExamples.prompt: Look at an orange and a box of dried dates. Which one can roll, and which one can stack neatly in a pile?
workedExamples.solution: The orange is a sphere — curved all over — so give it a push and it rolls away. The box of dates has flat faces, so it does not roll; it can be stacked neatly with other boxes.

workedExamples.title: Sorting home objects into rolls and stacks
workedExamples.prompt: Find a football, a cooking pot lid, and a stack of anjero (flatbread) at home. Say whether each one rolls or stacks.
workedExamples.solution: The football is a sphere, so it rolls. The pot lid is flat and round like a cylinder’s end, so it can stack with other lids. The anjero pieces are flat and round, so they stack neatly on top of each other.

workedExamples.title: Why a ball is a sphere
workedExamples.solution: A ball is round all over with no flat parts and no corners, so it is a sphere.

workedExamples.title: Why a box is a cube
workedExamples.solution: A box has flat square faces on every side and straight edges where the faces meet, so it is a cube.

workedExamples.title: Counting sides and corners
workedExamples.prompt: Count the sides and corners of a square scarf and a triangle-shaped samosa. How many of each does every shape have?
workedExamples.solution: The scarf is a square: count its sides — one, two, three, four — and its corners — one, two, three, four. The samosa is a triangle: count its sides — one, two, three — and its corners — one, two, three.

workedExamples.title: How many sides a circle has
workedExamples.solution: A circle is round all the way around with no straight parts and no corners, so it has just 1 curved side.

practice.prompt: Look at an orange. Is it a sphere, a cube, or a cylinder?
practice.hint: Feel the orange all over — does it have any flat parts?

practice.prompt: How many flat faces does a die (a small cube) have?
practice.hint: Turn the die in your hand and touch each flat side as you count.

practice.prompt: Give a tin can a gentle push on its side. Does it roll or stay still?
practice.answer: It rolls, because the tin has a curved side.
practice.hint: Look at whether the can has any flat or curved parts touching the ground.

practice.prompt: Look at a round clock, a square window, and a triangle roof. Name each 2D shape.
practice.hint: Count the straight sides on each shape — the clock has none.

practice.prompt: Count the sides of a rectangle-shaped door and a square floor tile. How many sides does each one have?
practice.hint: Touch each side once as you count around the shape.
Think about which shapes roll and which have flat sides.

practice.prompt: Look at a football and a box of dates. Which one rolls and which one stacks?
practice.answer: The football rolls; the box of dates stacks.
practice.hint: A shape with a curved surface rolls; a shape with flat faces stacks.

practice.prompt: Write ROLL or STACK for a ball, a book, and a tin can.
practice.answer: Ball: roll. Book: stack. Tin can: both (rolls on its side, stacks on its end).
practice.hint: Check whether each object has a curved surface, flat faces, or both.
A ball is round all over with no flat parts.
A box has flat square faces on every side.

practice.prompt: Count the sides of a triangle and a rectangle drawn on paper. How many sides does each have?
practice.hint: Touch and count each straight side, starting from the same corner.
Trace around the circle with your finger — does it have any corners?

steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

rules.title: The Rolling and Stacking Rule
rules.text: This is a favourite, because you can test it. The rule is simple: a shape can roll if it has a curved surface, and a shape can stack if it has flat faces to sit on.

rules.title: Sorting and a Shape Hunt
rules.text: Make two spaces, then sort by one rule at a time and say the rule out loud: this pile is for shapes that can roll, this pile is for shapes that can stack. One rule at a time is what keeps a sort honest.
rules.grownUpGuide:
How to Teach It: Sorting and a Shape Hunt

How to teach it: Make two spaces on the floor or table (two mats, two hoops, or just two piles). Give the child a handful of objects and shape cards and ask them to sort by one rule at a time. Say the rule out loud: ‘This pile is for shapes that can roll. This pile is for shapes that can stack.’ Then go on a shape hunt around the home – a round plate, a rectangle door, a tin cylinder, the square of a floor tile. Naming shapes in real life is the strongest sign you truly understands them.

rules.title: Child as Teacher: Sorting in Reverse
rules.text: Be the teacher and sort a pile of objects, telling you their rule.

fluency.prompt: Name the 3D shape of a football.
fluency.hint: Think about whether it has any flat parts.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is calling it a circle — circle is the flat 2D shape you’d draw around it; the ball itself is a sphere because it is solid and round all over.

fluency.prompt: How many faces does a cube have?
fluency.hint: Turn the cube and count each flat side once.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children often stop at 4 because they only count the sides they can see from one angle — remind them to turn the cube and count the hidden top and bottom faces too.

fluency.prompt: Does a cylinder (like a tin can) roll, stack, or both?
fluency.answer: Both — it rolls on its curved side and stacks on its flat end.
fluency.hint: Try standing the tin up, then laying it on its side.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is saying a cylinder can only roll. Remember to test standing it on its flat end too — it stacks there just like a cube.

fluency.prompt: Name the 2D shape of a window that has four equal straight sides.
fluency.hint: Count the sides — are they all the same length?
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes say 'rectangle' for any four-sided shape. Remind them a square's four sides must all be the same length; if two are longer, it is a rectangle instead.

fluency.prompt: How many corners does a triangle have?
fluency.hint: Count each pointed corner as you touch it.
fluency.errorFeedback: Some children count a side twice as a corner. Remind them to touch one corner at a time, moving in one direction around the shape.

fluency.hint: Match each picture to the shape name it looks like.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes call the can 🥫 a circle because its end looks round. Remind them the whole object is a 3D cylinder — circle is only the flat shape of its end.

fluency.prompt: Does a book roll, stack, or both?
fluency.answer: Stack only — a book has flat faces and no curved surface.
fluency.hint: Check if the object has any curved or round parts.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children may guess 'roll' because a book can slide. Remind them rolling needs a curved surface, and a book's sides and covers are all flat.

fluency.prompt: Look at a cooking pot (cylinder shape). Write ROLL or STACK for it.
fluency.answer: Both — it rolls on its curved side and stacks upright on its flat base.
fluency.hint: Try both positions: lying down and standing up.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children often write only 'STACK' because they usually see pots standing upright. Remind them to also test laying the pot on its side.

fluency.hint: A ball has no flat parts anywhere.
fluency.errorFeedback: A common mistake is writing 'circle'. Remember that circle is the flat 2D shape, while the solid ball itself is a sphere.

fluency.hint: A box has flat square faces on every side.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes say 'square' because one face looks square. Remind them a square is flat and 2D, while the whole solid box is a cube.

fluency.prompt: Count the sides of a square scarf.
fluency.hint: Touch each side once, starting from the same corner.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes count a corner as an extra side. Remind them to touch along each straight edge, not the corner points, as they count.

fluency.hint: Trace around the circle — is there ever a corner?
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes answer '0 sides' because the side is curved, not straight. Remind them a circle does have one side — it is just curved all the way round instead of straight.

realProblems.hint: Look at the box's faces — are they flat squares?
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children may say 'square' instead of 'cube'. Remind them square is the flat shape of one face, but the whole solid box is a cube.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, a trader has a folded triangular flag and a square scarf for sale. Count the sides of each.
realProblems.hint: Touch and count each straight side on both items.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children often forget to count all four sides of the scarf if it is folded. Remind them to unfold it fully before counting.

realProblems.hint: A circle has no straight parts or corners.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children sometimes think a curved line does not count as a 'side'. Remind them a circle's one curved side is still a side, just not straight.

realProblems.hint: Count the flat square faces on the box.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children may confuse a box with a cylinder if it has a round label. Remind them to check the shape of the box itself, not the picture on it.

realProblems.prompt: At home, count the sides of a rectangular table top and a triangular slice of anjero.
realProblems.answer: Table top (rectangle): 4 sides. Anjero slice (triangle): 3 sides.
realProblems.hint: Touch each straight edge once as you count around the shape.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why a sphere rolls but a cube does not.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A sphere is curved all over with no flat parts, so it moves smoothly in any direction when pushed — that is why it rolls. A cube has six flat faces and straight edges, so it stays still when pushed and can be stacked instead.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain why a cylinder can both roll and stack.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A cylinder has two flat circular ends and one curved side in between. When it lies on its curved side, it rolls easily like a sphere. When it stands up on one of its flat circular ends, it stays still and can be stacked, just like a cube.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A ball and a tin can are both round in some way. Explain how a sphere is different from a cylinder.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A sphere, like a ball, is round all over and has no flat faces at all. A cylinder, like a tin can, has two flat circular faces at its ends and a curved surface in between. So a sphere has zero faces, but a cylinder has two.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Meeting 2D Shapes (circle, square, rectangle, triangle).
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A 2D shape is flat — you can draw it on paper, but you cannot pick it up. A circle is round with one curved side and no corners. A square has 4 equal straight sides and 4 corners. A rectangle also has 4 straight sides and 4 corners, but only the opposite sides are equal. A triangle has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Counting Sides and Corners; Straight or Curved.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To count sides, touch and count each one, starting from the same point so you do not go around twice: a circle has 1 curved side, a triangle has 3 straight sides, and a square and rectangle each have 4 straight sides. A shape’s corners are where two straight sides meet — a circle has none, because its one side is curved, not straight.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Sorting Shapes and Finding Them in Everyday Objects.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: To sort shapes, put them into groups that share the same property — for example, 'shapes that roll' and 'shapes that stack', or 'shapes with straight sides' and 'shapes with a curved side'. Say the sorting rule out loud, then place each object or shape card into the correct group and check by testing it, such as giving it a gentle push to see if it rolls.
